figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: GFlowQEC ($n=180$). Rows of slots are tuples, with grey slots fixed to the identity, and Tanner graphs are codes. (a) Training, with no oracle call: (1) a stored form $x$ with its score $s$ and a bias $\gamma$, which give its reward $R(x,\gamma)$, (2) augmented and, with probability $1/2$, mirrored by $M$ with $\gamma\mapsto-\gamma$, (3) read by the transformer (three blocks, causal mask shaded), which takes the bias as a condition $z$ on its start token, (4) the trajectory-balance loss, weighing $R(x,\gamma)$ against $Z_{\theta}(z)\,p_{\theta}$, and its gradient step (dashed). (b) Deployment: (1) the frozen policy at $\gamma=\pm 1$, (2) $\mu N$ drawn forms (Sec. 5.4), (3) the $N$ with the highest $\log p_{\theta}(x\mid z)$, (4) the oracle’s bound score and SAT certification, (5) the top-scoring codes outside the stored forms.
figures.headline: Training draws on stored codes with no oracle call, and deployment pays only for the highest-ranked draws.
citing_sentences: Fig. 1 shows its training and deployment.

abstract: Choosing a quantum error-correcting code for a real device means scoring candidates with circuit-level simulations so slow that only a few hundred can be run. So every evaluation counts, and a search is judged by how many good codes it finds per paid evaluation. Quantum LDPC codes built from a few group elements protect many logical qubits, but good ones are rare in a huge space. We introduce GFlowQEC, to our knowledge the first generative flow network (GFlowNet) for quantum code design. It builds a code one group element at a time and learns to propose codes in proportion to a power of their score. We train it once on scores from earlier searches, freeze it, and let it propose lifted-product codes with $180$ physical qubits, scored by their distances. Ranking ten of its draws per paid call, it finds more than twice as many new top-scoring codes (inequivalent to any it was trained on) as tuned parallel tempering, even when tempering starts from GFlowQEC’s training codes. It finds more than three and a half times as many as a supervised screen ranking ten random candidates per call. When both rank a hundred, the screen beats GFlowQEC, and does best ranking GFlowQEC’s draws. Soft Q-learning, which shares the GFlowNet’s optimal policy, does as well at one noise bias and better at the other, so the gain does not depend on the GFlowNet’s training loss. Trained proposers can make a budget of expensive evaluations go further when good codes are rare.

sections.body: Quantum LDPC codes can protect many logical qubits in one block, and many are specified by a short list of group elements. Designing one is a search over lists, which is hard because the space is enormous and every candidate must be scored by its distance or by simulated failure rate. For a particular device, each candidate needs a circuit-level simulation taking minutes to hours, so a search scores only hundreds. The authors therefore count good codes found per paid call, meaning one oracle call on a code not yet scored in the run. A screen ranks random candidates, whereas a proposer draws good candidates directly, which matters when good codes are rare. GFlowNets sample objects in proportion to reward, so one model can yield many distinct good codes.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Good quantum codes are rare and each evaluation is costly, so a learned proposer may yield more good codes per call.

sections.body: Simple baselines are strong here: on hypergraph-product codes, a random walk matches simulated annealing and reinforcement learning at a matched budget. Reinforcement learning has built codes of up to 20 physical qubits with one logical qubit, and a code on nine physical qubits with its encoder. Language-model searches were not reimplemented, because their oracles and budgets differ and their models may have seen published codes. On a tree, GFlowNet training is equivalent to entropy-regularised reinforcement learning such as soft Q-learning. Conditional GFlowNets take a reward parameter as input. GFlowQEC adds conditioning on the noise bias and ranks its own draws at deployment. GFlowNets have been applied to quantum circuits, but not yet to code design.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior searches include strong simple baselines, and GFlowNets have so far been applied to circuits rather than codes.

sections.body: A CSS code is given by two binary check matrices, `H_X` and `H_Z`, which are valid exactly when their product is zero mod 2. Its number of logical qubits k equals n minus the ranks of the two matrices, and its distance is the lightest undetected pattern that changes the encoded information. The family here is built from a tuple of ten elements of the group Z6 times S3, which has 36 elements, through a lifted product. This gives 180 physical qubits, checks of weight 9, and k at least the group order. The authors drop a requirement of the original mitten construction that held for only 123 of 595 choices, so their family is much larger and includes codes with k above the group order.
sections.heading: Background
sections.headline: Lifted-product codes over a 36-element group give 180 physical qubits from ten group elements.

sections.body: Equivalent tuples are reduced to a canonical form by reordering and translation, and repeated forms are answered from memory at no cost. The score is the smaller of two terms, each a coefficient times a distance, so it counts orders of magnitude of suppression for the likelier failure. The top-scoring threshold is the highest score in a reference sample of 666 uniform draws with exact distances, 10.0 at bias plus or minus one, reached by 6 of the 666. At bias zero, 116 of the 666 share the highest score, so that threshold would not separate methods. A bound score takes 0.8 s in the median on one CPU core, while exact ladders take about 10 s on a uniform draw.
sections.heading: Search Space and Oracle
sections.headline: Codes are scored by a failure exponent from their distances, with a top-scoring threshold of 10.0 at bias plus or minus one.

sections.body: The policy is a causal transformer that fills ten slots in order, the five elements g and then the five elements h, with the first g and first h fixed to the identity. A mask keeps the elements of each sum distinct. It is trained with trajectory balance so that the probability of a tuple is proportional to its reward, a power of its clamped score, here with exponent 8 chosen by a fixed rule. Training uses scores that 42 earlier runs had paid for, with no oracle call during training. The network has three blocks of width 128 and four heads. At deployment, the frozen policy draws until it holds a multiple of the budget N of distinct forms, ranks them by log-probability, and pays for the top N. Ranking beat paying in draw order by more than five and a half times.
sections.heading: GFlowQEC
sections.headline: GFlowQEC builds each tuple one slot at a time and trains on stored scores with no new oracle calls.

sections.body: Every method uses the same oracle, search space and budget, with runs paired by seed. Tuned parallel tempering runs eight chains of local search, using the better of two temperature ranges, and a variant starts its chains from stored forms. The supervised screen regresses the scores of stored forms and ranks ten or a hundred times N uniform candidates. Soft Q-learning trained offline uses the same stored scores and network as the policy, so it tests whether the training objective matters. A quality-diversity evolutionary search and Bayesian optimisation are also run. The main measure is the number of certified top-scoring codes in each run's first N paid calls. Ratios pool seeds and use a 95 per cent log-ratio interval, and two methods are not separated when that interval contains 1.
sections.heading: Experimental Setup
sections.headline: The policy is compared with tuned parallel tempering, a supervised screen, soft Q-learning and other searches at matched budgets.

sections.body: Table 2 reports certified top-scoring codes per run at both biases. The policy found 313 and 317 codes, the screen at ten draws per call found 87 and 84, and tuned parallel tempering without stored data found 97 and 84. Soft Q-learning trained offline found 1.01 and 1.15 times the policy's count, ahead only at bias minus one. At ten draws per call the policy found 3.6 and 3.8 times as many as the screen. At a hundred draws per call the screen found more in every seed, and the policy found 0.45 and 0.62 times its count. Ranking the policy's draws instead of uniform candidates lifted the screen to 1.27 and 1.30 times its count. In the policy's runs, 87 to 93 per cent of neighbourhoods also hold a stored top-scoring code.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: The policy finds 2.4 and 2.8 times as many inequivalent top-scoring codes as tuned parallel tempering; a screen wins at a hundred draws.

sections.body: A trained proposer should pay off when good codes are too rare to sample, no cheap quantity ranks them, oracle calls are costly, and training is shared across searches. At 180 physical qubits good codes are not rare enough, which likely explains why a screen with a hundred random draws per call overtakes the policy. The number of logical qubits does not single out top-scoring codes: sorting stored scores by k would raise their top-scoring share by at most 1.4 times. The gain is in good codes per budget, not in the best code, and the paper shows no code better than those from other searches. Uniform sampling found about ten top-scoring codes in the same budget of paid calls. The score uses distances only, with no decoder, so the effect of circuit-level noise is unmeasured.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: The lead holds per paid call but vanishes per CPU second of exact ladders.

sections.body: Trained once on stored scores and used frozen at 180 physical qubits, the policy found more than twice as many top-scoring codes per paid call as tuned parallel tempering, counting inequivalent codes only. Soft Q-learning did as well or better, so the gain lies in the candidates rather than the training loss. Future work would re-score the top-scoring codes under circuit-level noise to see whether their ranking survives. A policy conditioned on measured noise could propose new codes after each calibration. The authors also suggest a compiler that selects codes from application and hardware specifications, with hard constraints built into the mask and the noise model entering as the condition.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: A frozen policy finds more inequivalent top-scoring codes per paid call, but circuit-level noise remains untested.
